title: Yoga Flow with Sheila Kelley
description: This 60 minute Yoga Flow class is ideal for beginners. It opens with some breath work and a gentle warm up followed by flowing poses for strengthening, stability and flexibility. Breathing and functional movement are focused on throughout the class. The flowing style leaves room for students to make choices that feel good for their bodies and weekly classes will likely have some variability. Because yoga is an individualized practice, participants are encouraged to focus on their own bodies and needs - to always do what feels good for them! It is always advised that participants consult with their medical provider prior to starting any new exercise regime. About the Instructor: Sheila Kelley successfully completed LPY Yoga’s 200-hour yoga teacher training program, which is registered with the Yoga Alliance. She is honored to have the opportunity to share your yoga practice and journey. Please bring your own yoga mat. Registration is not required, but please keep in mind that space is limited. title: Enchanted Pages Society
description: Join us at 7 PM in the Stoneham Room for our magical fantasy book club, The Enchanted Pages Society! In this group we will read and discuss fantasy books. The October title is Weavingshaw by Heba Al-Watsity. Pick up your copy at the circulation desk! "Three years ago, Leena Al-Sayer awoke with a terrible power. She can see the dead. Since then, she has hidden herself from the world, knowing that if she ever reveals her curse she will be locked away in an asylum. When her beloved brother, Rami, falls fatally ill, Leena is faced with a terrible CHOICE: Let him die or buy the expensive medicine that will save his life by bartering the only valuable thing she has—her secret. The Saint of Silence, a ruthless merchant who trades in confessions and is shrouded in unearthly rumors of cruelty and power, accepts her bargain, for a deadly price. Leena must find the ghost of Percival Avon, the last lord of Weavingshaw—or lose her freedom to the Saint forever. As Leena’s search takes her and the Saint to Weavingshaw, she finds the estate and the surrounding moors to be living things—hungry for blood and sacrifice. Fighting against Weavingshaw’s might, Leena must also fight her growing pull toward the enigmatic Saint himself, whose connection to Percival Avon remains a mystery. As the house begins to entomb them, time is running out on their desperate hunt for answers. For Leena has come to see that here in Weavingshaw, the dead are not hushed—and some secrets are better left buried with them." Questions? Contact Anna Powers at (781) 431-1324 or apowers@noblenet.org. People ages 16 and up are welcome. title: Kelly & Zach Weinersmith Author Talk
description: Join us for an out-of-this-world conversation with New York Times bestselling authors Kelly and Zach Weinersmith as they dive into their book, A City on Mars: Can We Settle Space, Should We Settle Space, and Have We Really Thought This Through? Earth is not well. The promise of starting life anew somewhere far, far away—no climate change, no war, no doomscrolling—beckons, and settling the stars ﬁnally seems within our grasp. Or is it? Critically acclaimed, bestselling authors Kelly and Zach Weinersmith set out to write the essential guide to a glorious future of space settlements, but after years of research, they aren’t so sure it’s a good idea. In a world hurtling toward human expansion into space, A City on Mars investigates whether the dream of new worlds won’t create nightmares, both for settlers and the people they leave behind. In the process, the Weinersmiths answer every question about space you’ve ever wondered about, and many you’ve never considered: Can you make babies in space? Should corporations govern space settlements? What about space war? Are we headed for a housing crisis on the Moon’s Peaks of Eternal Light—and what happens if you’re left in the Craters of Eternal Darkness? Why do astronauts love taco sauce? Speaking of meals, what’s the legal status of space cannibalism? With deep expertise, a winning sense of humor, and art from the beloved creator of Saturday Morning Breakfast Cereal, the Weinersmiths investigate perhaps the biggest questions humanity will ever ask itself—whether and how to become multiplanetary. Register today to be a part of the discussion! All SPL Virtual Talks are brought to you by the Friends of the Stoneham Library! See upcoming events here. See past event recordings here. title: Paul Vigna Author Talk
description: Join us for an eye-opening conversation with veteran journalist Paul Vigna as we examine his provocative book, The Almightier: How Money Became God, Greed Became Virtue, and Debt Became Sin, in which he explores the question: how did money go from a tool of commerce into the dominant faith of modern society? In The Almightier, Vigna takes readers on a sweeping historical journey from Renaissance Florence to today’s global financial markets, revealing how wealth accumulation evolved from a moral failing into an unspoken civic virtue. He uncovers the forgotten history of money, tracing the uneasy and often accidental alliance between wealth and religion as it developed from ancient city-states to today’s secular world, where religious devotion has receded and greed has stepped in to fill the void. Through engaging anecdotes, original research, and fresh perspectives on the causes of the many challenges we face today, Vigna makes a compelling argument that money has no power apart from the power we give it. Whether you are interested in economic history, personal finance, or the hidden cultural forces shaping modern life, this talk is sure to pique your interest. Register today to learn more about how devotion to money has replaced religion as the foundation of our society. All SPL Virtual Talks are brought to you by the Friends of the Stoneham Library! title: Rebecca Roanhorse Author Talk
description: Step into a sprawling world of celestial magic, political intrigue, and ancient prophecies with New York Times bestselling author Rebecca Roanhorse as we dive deep into her acclaimed Between Earth and Sky trilogy. Black Sun, Fevered Star, and Mirrored Heavens are inspired by the rich and diverse cultures of the pre-Columbian Americas, reshaping modern speculative fiction with unmissable worldbuilding. Black Sun, the first book in the trilogy, introduces us to the holy city of Tova. The winter solstice is usually a time for celebration and renewal, but this year it coincides with a solar eclipse, a rare celestial event proscribed by the Sun Priest as an unbalancing of the world. Meanwhile, a ship launches from a distant city bound for Tova and set to arrive on the solstice. The captain of the ship, Xiala, is a disgraced Teek whose song can calm the waters around her as easily as it can warp a man’s mind. Her ship carries one passenger. Described as harmless, the passenger, Serapio, is a young man, blind, scarred, and cloaked in destiny. As Xiala well knows, when a man is described as harmless, he usually ends up being a villain. Whether you are a longtime fan of the trilogy or searching for your next immersive fantasy read, this is an event you won’t want to miss out on. Register today to go behind the scenes with one of speculative fiction's most exciting voices! All SPL Virtual Talks are brought to you by the Friends of the Stoneham Library! title: Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery at the Central Library, which is closed until October 30. When it reopens, the gallery will have new hours, shown below. While it is closed, gallery tours for adult patrons are temporarily paused. Monday: ClosedTuesday: 12 pm – 6 pmWednesday: 12 pm - 6 pmThursday: 12 pm – 6 pmFriday: 10 am – 5 pmSaturday: 10 am – 5 pmSunday: Closed Maps trace out the complicated history of places, and we can use them to document geography in much the same way that we can use diaries and letters to document biography. In the eight cases of this exhibition, we follow the changing spatial forms of the place we now call Boston—from before the landscape carried that name all the way through the struggles, clashes, and dreams that continue to reshape the city today. These maps don’t merely depict facts about how the city looked at different moments in its history. Instead, they invite us to contemplate how geographic forces, both natural and human, have constructed the physical and social world around us, through large and small transformations that have transpired over many centuries. The Leventhal Map & Education Center regularly mounts exhibitions in our gallery, located in the historic McKim Building in the Boston Public Library in Copley Square. All of our exhibitions feature scholarly research as well as activities for families, children, and educators. Our permanent exhibit, Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City, is available any time our public gallery is open. Visit the digital exhibition to Becoming Boston here. title: Lexicon
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] July 2026Aluminum · 18 × 18 × 2 ftAlfonso Parra Rubio · Erik StrandMIT Center for Bits and Atoms Lexicon is a free-form structural shell built from individual origami-folded cells assembled into a two-sided lattice, or interlocking framework. The folding and assembling process creates a structure that is as strong and rigid as typical building methods, but it is much lighter. The structure is made for this space, Deferrari Hall. Its light, curved shape contrasts with the Boylston Street Building's heavy and blocky brutalist architecture. Lexicon's three pointed shape is a reference to Rafael Guastavino's tiled ceilings in the Central Library's McKim Building. By bringing together influences from both of the Central Library's buildings, Lexicon celebrates the role of geometry in design and construction. A collaboration between the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the Boston Public Library (BPL), and the Mayor's Office of Arts and Culture (MOAC). With Riccardo Foschi (University of Bologna), Rupert Malec (University of Innsbruck), Tomohiro Tachi (University of Tokyo), and Neil Gershenfeld (MIT Center for Bits and Atoms). Made possible and funded by MOAC.

title: Exhibition: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] To mark the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the Boston Public Library's Community History Department partnered with Revolutionary Spaces to offer a free and public program series called "Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness." Named for the unalienable rights identified in the Declaration—rights that inherently belong to all human beings, and that governments are created to protect—these programs brought people together to explore, question, and find inspiration in the Declaration of Independence. During two printmaking workshops--offered in partnership with the Arts Department and local artist Crystalle Lacouture—and four declaration writing workshops, library visitors reflected on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution. Displayed together, the art prints and writing pieces made by community members speak to the ongoing American struggle to create and sustain a free society. As a viewer of the exhibition, we invite you to consider: How do I identify with this nation's founding document? What do I celebrate? How do I use my voice in protest? About Community History The BPL Community History Department aims to democratize the expression of history by supporting people in their efforts to document the stories of themselves and their communities. We offer resources, programs, and support for local and community history work based on people’s lived experiences, knowledge, and expertise. About Revolutionary Spaces Revolutionary Spaces stewards the historic Old South Meeting House and Old State House as landmarks, museums, and active civic spaces. Its mission is to bring people together to explore the American struggle to create and sustain a free society—using history as a powerful tool for civic engagement and public dialogue. For more information, visit RevolutionarySpaces.org or follow them on social media at @RevSpaces. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Karin A. Martin - Get Plum Island!
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join University of Michigan professor Karin A. Martin for a conversation about her new book Get Plum Island!: Place and Politics in Massachusetts’s Ten-Year Fight Over the Parker River National Wildlife Refuge. The book tells the story of how the USFWS became interested in establishing a national wildlife refuge in Massachusetts, why Essex County became a premiere location, and how local communities and the state nearly succeeded in having the refuge abolished. Instead, after rounds of Congressional hearings and pocket veto by President Truman, a compromise was reached, reducing the refuge to about half its original size, and yet preserving the wonderful, vibrant refuge we know today. ​Karin A. Martin is the Mark A. Chesler Collegiate Professor of Sociology at the University of Michigan. She grew up in Amesbury, MA, received a BA from Hampshire College, and a PhD in Sociology from the University of California at Berkeley. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: How'd I Get Here?: Navigating the Arts in Boston with Ja'Hari Ortega
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Calling all local artists! Come chat with artist Ja'Hari Ortega about her experience securing fellowships, residencies, and exhibition opportunities in the Boston area. Community discussion is part of the program, so come with questions and a willingness to share your own experience, as well! Ja’Hari Ortega (she/her) is a multidisciplinary Boston-based artist, educator, and advocate who uses a vernacular language to capture the pulse of her city. Primarily drawn to metal sculpture, jewelry-making, and performance, Ortega received her BFA from the nation’s first and only public independent college of art and design, Massachusetts College of Art and Design, followed by a diploma in jewelry-making & repair from the longest continually operating trade school in the U.S., the North Bennet Street School. Ortega finds joy in using her artistic practice to engage and support her community: as one example, she was a panelist for Radical Imagination for Racial Justice, an initiative which invites Boston-based artists and creatives of color to imagine and co-create justice with their communities. Since graduating Ja'Hari has exhibited works in various galleries and showcases across multiple states, participated in numerous residencies and fellowships, and has taught art focused classes and workshops for all ages. The residencies and fellowships include Surf Point in Maine (2023), the Atlantic Center for the Arts in Florida (2023), Monson Arts in Maine (2024), and the Creative Entrepreneur Fellowship for the Arts & Business Council of Greater Boston (2025). title: Music Production with Hamstank: Beats, Recording, Mixing, & Mastering [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. title: Author Talk: Courtney Humphries - Climate Change and the Future of Boston
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us as author Courtney Humphries discusses her new book on the climate impacts facing Boston and the city’s efforts to mitigate and adapt to a changing climate.Like many of the world’s iconic coastal cities, Boston faces potentially severe impacts from climate change. Depending on global emissions, Boston could face several feet of sea level rise this century, which would leave many parts of the city subject to tidal and storm flooding. Precipitation events could become more frequent and extreme, and its already-humid summers could become dangerously hot, with most days over 90 degrees. Today, Boston is a booming city with a growing population, a glittering new waterfront neighborhood, world-class universities and a strong economy. Its future risks and opportunities related to climate change are shaped by the 400-year environmental, social and economic history of the city’s development. Climate Change and the Future of Boston describes how Boston’s history and current context shape future climate impacts and examines the mitigation and adaptation strategies the city has taken. Boston is a leader in acknowledging the problem of climate change; it has set a goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2050, among other climate-related goals. It has also developed science-based climate models and undertaken a robust planning process to identify strategies to protect its waterfront from flooding and increase its resilience to other climate-related impacts. Its mayor has embraced a progressive Green New Deal for Boston emphasizing the need for an inclusive and equitable approach to climate mitigation and adaptation. But the city also faces structural challenges, such as aging infrastructure, historic racial inequities, rising gentrification and income inequality and ongoing political and regulatory obstacles that hinder efforts to adapt in an efficient and just manner. She will conclude with a set of forward-looking scenarios about what the future may have in store for the city and the lessons it holds for other coastal cities struggling with these challenges.Courtney Humphries, PhD, is an interdisciplinary scholar, teacher, and award-winning journalist writing about science and the urban environment. title: Author Talk: Peggy Levitt - Move Over, Mona Lisa
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for an author talk and signing with Peggy Levitt, Wellesley College professor and renowned sociologist. In her new book, Move Over, Mona Lisa, Peggy asks: If the public is loudly calling for a wider range of art, literature, and ideas in our museums, libraries, and classrooms, why are our cultural and educational institutions so slow in making the change? Her answer is what she calls the "inequality pipeline," the layers of obstacles that keep art and ideas from circulating freely across the globe. Drawing on conversations with artists, writers, and cultural professionals in Argentina, Lebanon, and South Korea, Peggy shows that many of them have stopped waiting for old gatekeepers to change and are instead building new, alternative hubs and pathways that let art and ideas travel from cities like "Buenos Aires to Mexico City without having to pass through Madrid." Peggy takes us from the studios and desks where art and ideas are first created, through the museums and institutions that circulate and exhibit them, to the classrooms where they're researched and taught. Along the way, she reveals how cities, museums, and libraries influence more about both what creatives do and what the public learns than we might generally assume. The result is a hopeful, sharply observed new theory of how global cultural and intellectual change really happens. Peggy Levitt is the Mildred Lane Kemper Chair of Sociology at Wellesley College. She is also a co-founder of the Global (De)Centre. Her latest book, Move Over, Mona Lisa: Reimagining What We Read, Look At, and Learn was published this year by Stanford University Press. Peggy has previously written on social protections across borders, museums as site of immigration and national story-building, the influence of immigration on religion, and the socio-political realities of 1st and 2nd generation American immigrants. She co-directed the Transnational Studies Initiative and the Politics and Social Change Workshop at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University and the Hauser Center for Nonprofit Organizations at the Harvard Kennedy School from 1998 to 2020. title: Author Talk: Nicholas Boggs — Baldwin: A Love Story
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in person or online over Zoom Webinar to hear author Nicholas Boggs speak about his recent bestselling biography of James Baldwin, Baldwin: A Love Story, in celebration of LGBTQ+ History Month! Joining Nicolas in Conversation is author and professor, Jesse McCarthy. After the hour-long talk, Nicholas Boggs will sign copies of Baldwin during a signing facilitated by our local, independent bookseller, Trident Booksellers. Nicholas Boggs is the author of the New York Times bestselling biography, Baldwin: A Love Story (FSG, 2025), winner of the National Book Critics Circle John Leonard Prize, the PEN/Jacqueline Bograd Weld Award for Biography, the Stonewall/Israel Fishman Nonfiction Award, and the Randy Shilts Nonfiction Award. It was named a Top Ten Book of 2025 by Time Magazine and The Atlantic, and a New York Times Notable Book of the year. In addition, it was recognized with an Audie Award for Best Audiobook in History/Biography. Also the co-editor of Baldwin's collaboration with French artist Yoran Cazac, Little Man, Little Man: A Story of Childhood (2018), Boggs' research and writing have been supported by fellowships from the National Endowment for the Humanities, the National Humanities Center, the Gilder Lehrman Center and Beinecke Library at Yale, the Scholars-in-Residence Program at the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, and the Leon Levy Center for Biography, as well as a 2023 Whiting Creative Nonfiction Grant. He was educated at Yale (BA), American University (MFA), and Columbia (PhD). He lives in New York City. Jesse McCarthy is John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Humanities and of the Social Sciences at Harvard University. He is the author of The Blue Period: Black Writing in the Early Cold War, Who Will Pay Reparations on My Soul? and a novel, The Fugitivities. His writing on literature, politics, and the arts has appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Nation, and The New York Review of Books. He also serves as an editor at the magazines The Point and Public Books. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. In this two-hour role-playing game, you'll battle giant moths and monsters, solve puzzles, and work together with your group to help save the people of The Loom. title: Oral History Live: Black Trans Boston
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Queer History Boston for an Oral History Live panel discussion! Oral History Live: Black Trans Boston brings together leaders and organizers who have shaped the city's Black trans communities from the 1990s to today. Panelists trace this history from the founding of Trans Day of Remembrance in 1999 — a moment of collective mourning, visibility, and political awakening — through decades of organizing that followed. Grounded in oral history as both method and practice, this event offers a chance to listen deeply, honor lived experience, and recognize Black trans leadership as foundational to LGBTQ+ Boston's past, present, and future. Doors of Rabb Hall will open at 5:30 pm. The program will begin promptly at 5:45 pm with a remembrance ceremony led by Justice Roe Williams. This program is generously funded by the Howard Cooper LGBTQ+ Endowment Fund. Photo: Chastity Bowick with megaphone outside of Boston Police Department, Trans Resistance March. Photo provided by Queer History Boston.

description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. title: Handwriting the Constitution
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Patrons and visitors are invited to handwrite the U.S. Constitution in Bates Hall at the Central Library in Copley Square. This program aims to create time and a quiet space to reflect and deepen one's understanding of this historic document. All supplies will be provided. Participants will first stop by the supply table outside of Bates Hall to pick up writing supplies and a copy of the Constitution, before proceeding to Bates Hall. Reproductions of John Adams's personal copy of the Constitution held by Special Collections will also be available to transcribe. This program is self-paced. Patrons are invited to stay for the whole session or simply stay as long as they would like. About Handwriting the Constitution Handwriting the Constitution is a social art project begun in 2017 by artist Morgan O'Hara. It invites people from all walks of life to meet in public spaces to handwrite the U.S. Constitution or other documents written to protect human rights and freedoms. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Linford D. Fisher — Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in U.S. History
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join author Linford Fisher in a discussion of his book, Stealing America, where he shows that although the first enslaved Africans arrived in Jamestown in 1619, European slavery in America began more than a century before. The enslavement of Indigenous people began in the years just after 1492, ensnaring an estimated three to six million Natives throughout the Americas. Although largely erased from the public consciousness, Native enslavement continued for centuries to become a colossal phenomenon that affected nearly 600,000 Native Americans in North America alone, revealing the shocking truth that American colonizers enslaved Natives in roughly the same numbers as they imported enslaved Africans. From Virginia to California, from New England to Barbados, Stealing America traces the history of Indigenous enslavement and land dispossession, detailing how colonizers captured Natives and often deliberately mislabeled them as Black slaves to avoid detection. While the American Revolution pealed the bells of freedom for colonists, it paved a larcenous trail of westward expansion that subsequently plundered Indigenous land and stole the labor of Natives from nations like the Cherokee, Navajo, Nisean, and many others. “This double theft,” Fisher writes, “was central to the origins, growth, and eventual success of the English colonies and the United States—not just initially but throughout all of American history.” Fisher will weave together accounts of major episodes in American history including early colonization, the American Revolution, and the Civil War with lesser-known stories of Native enslavement and land loss. Fisher upends conventional histories about the nature of American slavery, revealing enslaved Natives in places we have overlooked, including southern antebellum plantations and the nineteenth-century American West. After Congress outlawed Native slavery in 1867, Americans forced Indigenous children into boarding schools and white homes, where they labored under forced assimilation. This practice was not reformed until the latter twentieth century, when Native nations finally secured increasing rights and self-determination. Linford D. Fisher is an associate professor of history at Brown University. The author of The Indian Great Awakening and principal investigator of the Stolen Relations project, he lives in Providence, Rhode Island. title: Music Production with Hamstank: Beats, Recording, Mixing, & Mastering [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. To request a disability accommodation and/or language services, contact teencentral@bpl.org. title: 2026 Druker Award Lecture: Can Architecture Change A City?
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Please join us in person or online over Zoom Webinar for the 2026 Druker Award presentation and talk with KPMB Architects’ Marianne McKenna and Paulo Rocha. This 2026 Druker Award lecture explores how cities are continually reshaped, with KPMB Architects’ Marianne McKenna and Paulo Rocha examining Boston’s evolution and the story behind Boston University’s Duan Family Center for Computing & Data Sciences. Through the lens of this landmark project, they’ll consider how the design process and partnership can create lasting social, environmental, and economic impact. They’ll also look to the future of architecture in Boston. About the Presenters Marianne McKenna, Founding Partner, KPMB ArchitectsMarianne McKenna, the 2025 RAIC Gold Medalist, is a founding partner of KPMB Architects and an Officer of the Order of Canada. She is internationally known for her leadership on major cultural landmarks, including the Royal Conservatory of Music’s TELUS Centre for Performance and Learning and Koerner Hall, the revitalization of Toronto’s historic Massey Hall, the renewal of Orchestra Hall in Minneapolis, and the Jenny Belzberg Theatre at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity. Her approach balances deep respect for architectural legacy with contemporary interventions that support new uses, improved performance, and broader public access. She is a passionate advocate for design excellence, sustainability, and community‑building through architecture. Paulo Rocha, Partner, KPMB ArchitectsPaulo Rocha is a partner at KPMB Architects whose work is defined by a rigorous approach to design, materiality, and craft. Since joining the firm in 1995, he has played a leading role in shaping many of KPMB's most recognized projects across cultural, academic, workplace, residential, and civic sectors. His expertise spans the full lifecycle of a project, combining strong design leadership with technical precision to ensure architectural vision is carried through construction. His portfolio includes the Governor General's Medal-winning Remai Modern, the RIBA Award-winning Gardiner Museum renewal, the Rotman School of Management Expansion, and Boston University's Duan Family Center for Computing & Data Sciences, one of the largest fossil fuel-free buildings in the Boston area. He is currently leading the design of the Montreal Holocaust Museum and the Vancouver Art Gallery. The Druker Award is presented annually to a speaker or speakers who has or have made outstanding and important contributions to the world of urban art, architecture, and design. The award is a reproduction of the historic copper griffins gracing the roofline of the Boston Public Library’s iconic McKim Building. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Lauren Klein and Tanvi Sharma on "Data by Design"
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join visualization historian Lauren Klein and designer Tanvi Sharma for a conversation about their new book Data by Design: Visualization and Power from Abolition to the Dawn of Data Science. The book returns to the history of data visualization to expose the power of charts and maps—and to show how they can be used for social change. Lauren and Tanvi will be in conversation with Arvind Satyanarayan, a professor of data visualization at MIT. ​Lauren Klein is Professor of Data & Decision Sciences and English at Emory University, where she also directs the Digital Humanities Lab and the Atlanta Interdisciplinary AI Network. Her research brings together computational and critical methods to explore questions of gender, race, and justice, both in early America and today. Klein is the author (with Catherine D’Ignazio) of the award-winning Data Feminism (MIT Press, 2020), and the editor (with Matthew K. Gold) of Debates in the Digital Humanities (Univ. of Minnesota Press), among other publications. ​Tanvi Sharma is a design technologist working at the intersection of data, aesthetics, and the humanities. She is currently an Art Director at Apple and co-author of Data by Design (MIT Press, 2026). She has previously worked at Pentagram, Public Policy Lab, and Spotify. She lives in Harlem, NY, with her two cats, Yuchi and Bubbles. More at tanvi.network. ​Arvind Satyanarayan is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at MIT EECS, and leads the Visualization Group at the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). His research uses visualization as a petri dish to study intelligence augmentation (IA), or how computation can amplify our cognition and creativity, while respecting our agency. Open-source visualization systems developed by Arvind and his collaborators are widely used by researchers, companies, and journalists. Arvind’s research has been recognized with several awards including, most recently, an Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship.Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] What is copyright? What does it do? Why have I been told to “copyright” my work? Do I “own” copyright? Why does this matter? How We Can Help: The Boston Research Center helps bring Boston’s deep neighborhood and community histories to light through the creation and use of new technologies. title: Music Production with Hamstank: Beats, Recording, Mixing, & Mastering [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. title: Author Talk: Paul Lewis — How "The Raven" Became America's Most Famous Poem
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Boston College Professor Emeritus Paul Lewis in a discussion of his new book on Edgar Allan Poe's famous poem. In 1845, over 5,300 poems were published in American magazines. Most immediately began their deserved descent into oblivion. Poe's "Raven" stands as the most conspicuous exception to this. But why? What factors influenced the attention devoted to "The Raven" from the day when it was first published? Why was it widely reprinted, praised, criticized, and mocked during the next weeks and months? Why did it inspire parodies that replaced Poe's "saintly bird of yore" with a veritable menagerie of other animals—including an owl, gazelle, turkey, pig, dog, cats, rats, and (eek!) bedbugs? And how did Poe's reputation—as a literary brawler and harsh book reviewer and as a man who struggled with money and alcohol—play into the reception of "The Raven"? Signed copies of Paul Lewis' Quothing "The Raven" The First Responses to America's Most Famous Poem will be available at this book-launch event. Paul Lewis is a Professor Emeritus at Boston College, a past president of the Poe Studies Association, and the curator of exhibitions on literary Boston. As the Board of Directors chair of the Edgar Allan Poe Foundation of Boston, Inc., Lewis worked with others to celebrate Poe in the city of his birth by having a square at the intersection of Boylston Street and Charles Street South dedicated to Poe in 2010 and then installing a statue of Poe in it in 2014. title: Google Drive Made Easy: Store, Organize & Share Your Files
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Ready to tame the chaos of digital files? Join our 90-minute workshop to unlock the full potential of Google Drive. Whether you're a student, a creative professional, or a small business owner, this session is designed to transform the way you manage your documents, photos, and projects. We'll cover everything from the basics of file storage to advanced sharing and collaboration tools, helping you work smarter, not harder. In this hands-on workshop, you'll learn how to: Organize like a pro: Master folders, search functions, and file-naming strategies to find anything in seconds.Collaborate seamlessly: Share files and folders with specific permissions, and work together on documents in real-time.Streamline your workflow: Discover powerful integrations with other Google apps like Docs, Sheets, and Slides.Take your work anywhere: Learn how to access, edit, and sync your files across all your devices. Walk away with the confidence to use Google Drive as your central hub for all your work and personal projects. No prior experience is needed—just bring your enthusiasm and get ready to create your most productive digital workspace yet. Logistical Information To get the most out of this class, please ensure you have an active Google account you can log into. We will be using these accounts for hands-on activities and will not have time to set up new accounts during class. No need to bring a computer—we'll provide one for you! Feel free to bring a pen and notebook for taking notes. You're also welcome to follow along on your smartphone or other mobile device. Registration is highly encouraged. Please register at the bottom of the page. Walk-ins are welcome if space allows. Need help signing up or have questions? Give us a call at 617-859-2323 or send an email to computerworkshops@bpl.org. title: Music Production with Hamstank: Beats, Recording, Mixing, & Mastering [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. title: Boston Research Center Office Hours
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The Boston Research Center (BRC) is a digital community history and archives lab that supports Boston residents in telling the stories of their neighborhoods and communities. How We Can Help: The Boston Research Center helps bring Boston’s deep neighborhood and community histories to light through the creation and use of new technologies. The BRC can support your ideas and projects in many different ways. This support may look like: Offering free introductory workshops about digital humanities tools and methodsSharing resources and toolkits to help demystify digital projects and community history workConsulting on project design and maintenance Connecting community historians with subject experts, research resources, and grant opportunitiesProviding technical support for digital history projectsHelping promote events centered on community projects If you aren't sure what you need, drop in! title: Handwriting the Constitution
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Patrons and visitors are invited to handwrite the U.S. Constitution in Bates Hall at the Central Library in Copley Square. This program aims to create time and a quiet space to reflect and deepen one's understanding of this historic document. All supplies will be provided. Participants will first stop by the supply table outside of Bates Hall to pick up writing supplies and a copy of the Constitution, before proceeding to Bates Hall. Reproductions of John Adams's personal copy of the Constitution held by Special Collections will also be available to transcribe. This program is self-paced. Patrons are invited to stay for the whole session or simply stay as long as they would like. About Handwriting the Constitution Handwriting the Constitution is a social art project begun in 2017 by artist Morgan O'Hara. It invites people from all walks of life to meet in public spaces to handwrite the U.S. Constitution or other documents written to protect human rights and freedoms. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. To request a disability accommodation and/or language services, contact the department listed in the "Contact Info" pane on the right. Please allow at least two weeks to arrange accommodation. Programming at the Boston Public Library is funded through private support. To learn more about supporting the Library, please visit the Boston Public Library Fund's website.

title: Humanity of the Arts & Humanity of the Legal Services (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The internet is replete with legal information. Legal blogs, contract templates, statutes, cases and commentary, AI agents, etc. Why hire a lawyer when so many answers rest at your fingertips? title: Intro to Contracts & Negotiation (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] What is a contract? Are there things it must include? Do I need a lawyer to write or negotiate it for me? A contract exists when participants come together to exchange goods and services for compensation. A written contract is a valuable tool for any creative business. Contracts take all shapes and sizes, but the best contract is the one that all parties understand and that meets all parties’ business needs. Whether you routinely use contracts in your creative practice or you’re new to it, this workshop is for you! Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Copyright & Intellectual Property (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Copyright lasts a long time. For many creatives, the copyright on their works might last multiple lifetimes before it enters the public domain. This is why it’s so important for artists and creative workers to include copyright as part of their legacy plan. Who has the power to use, enjoy, publicize, and distribute your creative works?
